title: The Dark Side of Flow: Passive Flow State, Metacognitive Bias, and Compulsive Use of Short-Form Videos
authors: Na Wang, Long Ma, Chei Sian Lee
abstract: This study examines why short-form videos (SFVs) in social media foster compulsive use by reconceptualizing flow in low-effort digital environments. While prior research has primarily highlighted flow’s optimal facets, this study argues that in passive media contexts, flow may also embody maladaptive qualities. Drawing on dual-process theory, SFV engagement is conceptualized as predominantly driven by intuitive processing in System 1 (heuristic processing related), through which flow weakens self-control monitoring of System 2 (systematic processing related). To capture the underlying psychological mechanisms, flow is reconceptualized as a passive psychological state comprising both immersive and maladaptive dimensions (i.e., concentration, enjoyment, telepresence, heightened arousal, affective reliance, and loss of self-reflection). In addition, the desirability- and feasibility-related cues embedded in digital environments are examined as heuristic triggers of passive flow state, while overestimation of self-control is conceptualized as a critical mediator linking flow to compulsive use. Survey data from 842 SFV users were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. The findings revealed that overestimation of self-control emerges as the strongest driver of compulsive use, exceeding the total effect of flow. Flow is found to both directly impact compulsive SFV use and indirectly through increasing the overestimation of self-control. At the subdimensional level, flow’s dimensions exert divergent effects, with concentration, telepresence, and affective reliance significantly intensifying compulsive use and/or overestimation of self-control. By integrating a dual-process perspective with a multidimensional conceptualization of flow, this study advances understanding of how passive flow state fosters metacognitive bias and compulsive engagement, offering theoretical and practical insights to promote more sustainable digital environments that support users’ well-being.

title: Internalized Cultural Heuristics of Warmth and Competence in Identity Labels: The Indirect Indexicality of Stereotype and Emotional Reaction Activation as a Function of Social Media Exposure
authors: Na Wang, Julius Matthew Riles, Alyssa Coffey, Can Liu
abstract: The stereotype content model (SCM) theorizes how stereotypic attribution profiles predict individuals’ emotional outcomes to social groups. However, how such culturally ingrained stereotypic attributions and emotional outcomes could be activated under minimal context media conditions (e.g., solely via identity label media exposure, with no additional identity content), merits investigation. In this research context, the semiotic construct of indirect indexicality is applied to the SCM to explore the activation and use of stereotype-based judgments under such conditions. Specifically, an experiment is conducted to examine how social media exposure to basic identity labels could activate heuristic stereotypical and emotional outcomes relative to a control baseline, with all other post content held constant. Results Results demonstrate that mere identity label exposure serves as a linguistic cue sufficient to enhance reliance on SCM attributions and emotional outcomes, relative to a baseline, when making broader group judgments. Furthermore, findings reveal emotional outcomes extending beyond SCM predictions. Moderating influences, including intergroup contact, are discussed.

title: Level Up Your Mood – Mood Repair Effects of Hedonic Versus Eudaimonic Video Games
authors: Gary L. Wagener, André Melzer
abstract: Abstract: Current research emphasizes the therapeutic potential of hedonic video games (VGs), designed for fun and entertainment, which, for example, reduce anxiety primarily through psychological detachment. However, eudaimonic experiences of deeper emotional engagement and meaning may have even stronger therapeutic effects. In this lab experiment ( N = 95), we compared hedonic and eudaimonic VG experiences with a non-gaming control group (jigsaw puzzling) to reduce anxiety and promote relaxation. Anxiety was induced with an autobiographical recall task. Next, participants were randomly assigned to their respective activity. The anxiety levels, self-reported relaxation, and physiological relaxation (heart rate variability) were measured throughout the entire time. Both game types reduced anxiety and increased relaxation, but only the eudaimonic game led to prolonged physiological relaxation. In contrast, jigsaw puzzling did not reduce anxiety and was linked to greater stress responses. These findings highlight the therapeutic value of eudaimonic VGs, warranting further investigation through longitudinal studies.

title: Is Information Verification Just a Matter of Intellectual Humility?
authors: Carmela Sportelli, Paolo Giovanni Cicirelli, Giuseppe Corbelli, Marinella Paciello, Francesca D’Errico
abstract: Abstract: Adolescents can be vulnerable to misinformation, facing the daily challenge of assessing false, inaccurate, or misleading news. Understanding the psychological processes contributing to this vulnerability is crucial for enhancing their information verification skills. Previous research has established a positive association between intellectual humility – the acknowledgment of the fallibility of one’s own beliefs – and the intention to verify misleading content. However, the underlying process through which it occurs remains underexplored. Intellectual humility may also be linked to moral disengagement: individuals characterized by an awareness of their own fallibility can be less inclined to rely on moral disengagement mechanisms, which serve as self-serving defensive justifications used to preserve a positive self-image when faced with moral transgressions, thereby being more likely to engage in rightful online behaviors. Therefore, our research aims to test the relationship between intellectual humility and the intention to verify online content, investigating the mediating role of moral disengagement. The study, conducted with 380 Italian adolescents ( M = 14.43, SD = 0.74), utilized a conversational web app to measure the variables of interest. The results show that moral disengagement fully mediates the relationship between intellectual humility and the intention to verify the information. This highlights the importance of fostering metacognitive abilities, such as self-reflection and the capacity to reconsider one’s own perspective, in promoting media literacy. These findings suggest that interventions aimed at enhancing intellectual humility may reduce moral disengagement toward fake news and promote more responsible online behavior. Limitations and directions for future research are also discussed.

title: From Structural Inequalities to Labor Precarity: Adoption of Digital and AI Tools in Latin American Journalism
authors: Miguel Garcés-Prettel, Jesús Arroyave-Cabrera, Summer Harlow, Lilian Kanashiro, Mariana De Maio, Janara Nicoletti, Adriana Amado, Dasniel Olivera Pérez, Martín Oller Alonso, Celeste González de Bustamante, Maximiliano Frías Vázquez, Víctor Quintanilla-Sangüeza
abstract: While inequalities in technological access and use have been widely documented, few studies have examined their link to labor precarity and social inequality in journalism in the Global South. This article analyzes this relationship through a multilevel study of Worlds of Journalism Study data from 4,250 journalists in 11 Latin American countries. Results show that macro-level inequality, measured by the Gini coefficient, is not associated with the use of advanced digital technologies, including AI, while micro-level precarity, expressed in contractual instability and excessive workloads, is. Working conditions, rather than national disparities, are key to explaining inequalities in technology adoption.

title: Does alternative news media inform or misinform voters during election campaigns?
authors: Atle Haugsgjerd, Rune Karlsen, Tine Figenschou, Karoline Andrea Ihlebæk, Toril Aalberg
abstract: A growing body of literature has studied the audiences and effects of alternative media use. We contribute by examining how such usage shapes political knowledge during election campaigns. Given their partisan orientation, lack of professional verification, and often provocative style, alternative media are found to produce and circulate misinformation, even as their users are often politically engaged, active news consumers. We ask whether alternative media inform rather than misinform citizens during election campaigns. Adopting a two-dimensional conception of political knowledge, we examine both surveillance knowledge and confidence in that knowledge – along with misinformation understood as the combination of the two. Utilizing individual-level panel data from Norway, our findings suggest that alternative news use is not associated with being better or worse informed, but with being more confident in one’s political knowledge. We discuss how these effects may differ in more polarized or lower-quality information environments.

title: Stop pushing junk science! User corrections of misinformation in science are common and sophisticated
authors: Tuomas Heikkilä
abstract: Misinformation is often equated with blatant falsehoods from dubious sources, overlooking that scientific sources, too, can accidentally publish inaccurate information to large online audiences. This article explores how social media users share, evaluate and address misinformation in science, defined as unreliable research rejected by relevant experts for violating scientific integrity. Using a mixed-methods analysis of Twitter discussions on retracted COVID-19 studies (33,730 tweets and 13,743 replies), the study found that, while most users accepted retracted science at face value, they were also disputed often, with user corrections accounting for nearly half of all replies. Corrections also closely mirrored established experimental recommendations, being mostly elaborative, non-confrontational, and commonly employed one or more debunking strategies. In contrast, polarising and overly convoluted language was rare. The results highlight the significant role that ordinary users play in countering unreliable science ‘in the wild’ and the need for researchers and policymakers to strengthen support for bottom-up corrective practices.

title: How Recipients Compose Their News Sources Online: Utilizing Tracking Data to Investigate Digital News Media Repertoires
authors: Robin Leuppert, Jule Scheper, Nico Spreen, Elena Link
abstract: Today’s high-choice media environment offers various opportunities for interest-driven news exposure, resulting in highly diverse and fragmented news usage patterns, especially in the digital media environment. Media repertoires provide a suitable theoretical framework for considering these circumstances and investigating the entirety and interrelatedness of individuals’ news sources, rather than focusing on singular news offerings. We explore media repertoires focusing on news by relying on behavioral tracking data from 805 German respondents over eleven weeks (November 2022–January 2023). Conducting a latent class analysis based on news usage frequencies across seventeen news categories, we identified eight digital news media repertoires with distinct usage patterns. Repertoire comparisons via analysis of variance (ANOVA) further revealed differences in the news topics used, users’ diversity of news outlets, news concentration, and news usage duration. Implications for future research on investigating media repertoire compositions are discussed.

title: An Experimental Comparison of AI-Enabled Semi-Structured Interviews and Fixed Surveys: Respondent Satisfaction, Response Patterns, Quality, and Representation
authors: Amanda Austin, Edward Hohe, Ryan Kennedy, Leib Litman, William Minozzi, Laura Moses
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) interviewing offers the potential to enhance the depth and quality of survey research, yet it may also introduce respondent fatigue and unintended consequences for the measurement of political attitudes. From the standpoint of respondents, more extensive interviews impose greater cognitive and temporal burdens, which may reduce engagement or increase satisficing. From the perspective of political behavior researchers, deeper probing may shift the subset of beliefs or arguments that respondents access when forming opinions, thereby altering the distribution and apparent stability of measured attitudes. To investigate these dynamics, we conduct a large-scale, fully randomized experiment. We find that AI-mediated interviewing significantly increases both the volume and specificity of respondents’ articulated rationales, but any decline in participant satisfaction is minuscule and we detect no increase in participant rolloff. However, AI interviews appear to shape subsequent responses: After offering justifications through AI interaction, respondents exhibit greater polarization in follow-up items. This result suggests that AI interviewing may alter the cognitive architecture of opinion formation. These findings both highlight the potential for AI interviewing and underscore the need for studies of how AI interviewing may become a source of attitudinal change.
